name: openkermit
desc: Scriptable network and serial communication for UNIX and VMS
why: Kermit is a forgotten serial and network file transfer protocol, and a scriptable implementation is a real door into retro comms.

brief.what_it_is: Open Kermit is the home of ongoing development of C-Kermit, a communications package with a text UI. Its parts include a portable scripting language that works like a shell but has built-in screen-scraping automation (similar in concept to expect) and built-in file transfer, an implementation of the Kermit file transfer protocol, a network client and server, a serial port interface, and a BBS client. The homepage says it runs on hundreds of platforms, from 1970s computers and 1990s pocket calculators to modern desktop and mobile OSes. The homepage text does not describe the inputs and outputs in detail.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents Kermit as a long-running communications tool that has been carried forward since 1981, starting at Columbia University, passing through the Kermit Project, and now continued by Open Kermit after one of Kermit's founders retired following 44 years. The site also says the earlier project websites remain online as a historical snapshot.
brief.install_notes: The homepage does not give installation steps. It points to a 'Getting Kermit and Downloads' page with links to GitHub source and binaries, covering modern and historical platforms. The Homebrew formula lists the executables as ckermit.ini, kermit, and kermit-sshsub, but I did not confirm those names from the homepage text.
brief.standout: Kermit is a serial and network file transfer tool with a scripting language built in, and it has been continuously developed since 1981 across three successive projects. The homepage says the earlier project sites are still online, which makes the history itself browsable.
brief.status: Active as far as the homepage shows: it describes Open Kermit as currently carrying the project forward and invites contributions, and it is managed by John Goerzen. I found no release date or last commit date because I did not reach the GitHub repository or the downloads page.
brief.caveats: I only read the homepage. The page text contains no install commands, no usage examples, and no link URLs beyond the homepage, so the docs and download pages were not checked. Its claim of running on hundreds of platforms is the project's own. The brew description and scout note describe it as a 'forgotten' protocol, which is the scout's framing and not the project's.

entry.title: Open Kermit
entry.tldr: C-Kermit, a serial and network communications package from 1981 with a built-in scripting language, file transfer protocol, and expect-style automation, still under active development.
entry.deeper_look:
Open Kermit is the current home of C-Kermit, a text-mode communications package. It bundles several things: an implementation of the Kermit file transfer protocol, a network client and server, a serial port interface, a BBS client, and a portable scripting language. The scripting language is described as "similar in concept to the shell, but with built-in screen-scraping automation like expect and built-in file transfer."

Kermit started at Columbia University in 1981. The homepage says Open Kermit is the third project to carry it forward, after the original Columbia effort and the Kermit Project. It was set up after one of Kermit's founders retired following 44 years. The earlier project sites are kept online as a historical snapshot, so the history can be browsed.

The idea underneath is that file transfer and terminal automation were once one problem, solved over unreliable serial lines between very different machines. Kermit is a protocol built for that world, and the same tool still talks to modern networks. The homepage claims it runs on hundreds of platforms, from 1970s computers and 1990s pocket calculators to current desktop and mobile systems. That claim is the project's own.

The Homebrew formula installs three executables: kermit, ckermit.ini, and kermit-sshsub. The homepage text does not describe inputs, outputs, or usage in detail, so the docs are the place to go after the first run.

entry.whats_unique: It combines a file transfer protocol, serial and network terminal, and an expect-style scripting language in one package, with a lineage that runs unbroken from 1981.
entry.caveats: The brief covers only the homepage, so usage examples, release dates, and the downloads page are unchecked.
